message.content: {"schema_version":"teaching-unit.v0.4.0","input_manifest_sha256":"b10e28e0e4452a02004d6f4088a30565320e7b30dbb79e37fdbe4ade1d739446","candidate_lineage_id":"2026-10-28-rdmv-ny-class-d:lineage:81","source_registry_sha256":"f5f0e765d8ae90e6aae6e6bbb4e1e1ba64f643ffc8ff14436ec954958fb7f36d","units":[{"unit_id":"sec04-u01","module_id":"sec04-m01","objective_ids":["sec04-u01"],"title":{"text":"Sign colors, stop and yield","fact_ids":["sec04-F01","sec04-F02","sec04-F03"]},"why_how":[{"text":"Sign shape and color announce each sign's job before you can read it.","fact_ids":["sec04-F01"]},{"text":"Stop and yield signs both make you give up the right-of-way, in different ways.","fact_ids":["sec04-F02","sec04-F03","sec04-R01"]}],"worked_example":{"scenario":{"text":"Eli reaches a stop sign at a corner where there is no stop line but there is a crosswalk.","fact_ids":["sec04-F02"]},"reasoning":{"text":"The stop sign demands a full stop before the stop line, else the crosswalk, else the nearest point with a clear view.","fact_ids":["sec04-F02"]},"result":{"text":"Eli stops fully before the crosswalk, yields, then goes when clear.","fact_ids":["sec04-F02"]}},"misconception":{"claim":{"text":"Common mistake: treating a yield sign as if it never requires stopping.","fact_ids":["sec04-F03"]},"correction":{"text":"A yield sign demands slowing, traffic checks and readiness to stop, and a full stop whenever conditions require.","fact_ids":["sec04-F03","sec04-R01"]}},"memory_support":{"text":"Stop always halts; yield halts when it must.","fact_ids":["sec04-R01"]},"self_check":{"prompt":{"text":"You come to a yield sign and cross traffic is approaching close by. What must you do?","fact_ids":["sec04-F03"]},"answer":{"text":"Slow down, be ready to stop, and stop fully if conditions require, yielding the right-of-way.","fact_ids":["sec04-F03"]},"rationale":{"text":"Yield halts only when traffic demands it, but it always yields right-of-way.","fact_ids":["sec04-R01","sec04-F03"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec04-u01-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"Reading signs at a glance","fact_ids":["sec04-F01","sec04-F02","sec04-F03","sec04-F04"]},"lines":[{"text":"Shape and color tell the job.","fact_ids":["sec04-F01","sec04-F02","sec04-F03","sec04-F04"]},{"text":"Stop, yield and regulation signs.","fact_ids":["sec04-F01","sec04-F02","sec04-F03","sec04-F04"]}],"narration":{"text":"This lesson begins the traffic control chapter with signs. The manual says sign shape and color announce what each sign does, so you can know its job even before you read the words. We will match the four main color families to their jobs, then look closely at two of the most important signs you will meet: the red-and-white stop sign and the red-and-white yield sign. They are often confused, so we will compare them directly. We finish with the other regulation signs, including the red circle with a slash. Later lessons cover warning, work, guide and service signs in more detail.","fact_ids":["sec04-F01","sec04-F02","sec04-F03","sec04-F04"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":41,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec04-u01-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Colors and shapes","fact_ids":["sec04-F01"]},"lines":[{"text":"Regulation: white rectangles, black or red.","fact_ids":["sec04-F01"]},{"text":"Warning: yellow diamonds, black.","fact_ids":["sec04-F01"]},{"text":"Destination green; services blue.","fact_ids":["sec04-F01"]}],"narration":{"text":"Start with the color code. Regulation signs, which state rules, are normally white rectangles with black or red markings. Warning signs are yellow diamonds with black markings. Destination signs are green with white markings. And service signs are blue with white markings. So before you are close enough to read the words, the color and shape already tell you whether a sign is stating a rule, warning you of a hazard, guiding you to a place, or pointing out a service. Practice naming the job from the color alone, because that is how the manual says signs announce themselves.","fact_ids":["sec04-F01"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec04-u01-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"The stop sign","fact_ids":["sec04-F02"]},"lines":[{"text":"Red and white; a full stop.","fact_ids":["sec04-F02"]},{"text":"Yield the right-of-way.","fact_ids":["sec04-F02"]},{"text":"Stop line, else crosswalk, else clear view.","fact_ids":["sec04-F02"]}],"narration":{"text":"The red-and-white stop sign demands a full stop, with the right-of-way yielded to others. Where you stop follows a set order. Stop before the stop line if there is one. If there is no stop line, stop before the crosswalk. If there is neither, stop at the nearest point where you have a clear view into the intersection. A slow roll is not a stop. Come to a full stop at the right point, yield to traffic and pedestrians who have the right-of-way, and go only when it is safe. Keep the three stopping points in order: line, crosswalk, clear view.","fact_ids":["sec04-F02"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec04-u01-s4","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"The yield sign","fact_ids":["sec04-F03"]},"lines":[{"text":"Red and white; slow down.","fact_ids":["sec04-F03"]},{"text":"Check traffic; be ready to stop.","fact_ids":["sec04-F03"]},{"text":"Stop fully when conditions require.","fact_ids":["sec04-F03"]}],"narration":{"text":"The red-and-white yield sign asks something different. It demands that you slow down, check traffic, and be ready to stop. You make a full stop whenever conditions require it, and you yield the right-of-way. So at a yield sign, you may not need to stop if the way is clear, but you must always slow, look and give way. If traffic is coming, you stop and wait. The yield sign is about readiness and giving way, while the stop sign, as we just saw, always requires a full stop. Both, though, end with you yielding the right-of-way to others.","fact_ids":["sec04-F03"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec04-u01-s5","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Stop versus yield","fact_ids":["sec04-R01","sec04-F02","sec04-F03"]},"lines":[{"text":"Stop: always a full halt.","fact_ids":["sec04-R01","sec04-F02","sec04-F03"]},{"text":"Yield: halt only when traffic demands.","fact_ids":["sec04-R01","sec04-F02","sec04-F03"]},{"text":"Stop order: line, crosswalk, sight point.","fact_ids":["sec04-R01","sec04-F02","sec04-F03"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is the trap. Because both signs are red and white and both involve yielding, people blur them. The manual draws the line clearly. A stop sign always means a full halt. A yield sign means a halt only when traffic demands it. Yet both yield the right-of-way, while at a stop sign you stop before the stop line, else the crosswalk, else the nearest point with a view of cross traffic. So the difference is whether the halt is automatic or conditional. If a question asks which sign always requires a full stop, the answer is the stop sign, never the yield sign.","fact_ids":["sec04-R01","sec04-F02","sec04-F03"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec04-u01-s6","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Other regulation signs","fact_ids":["sec04-F04"]},"lines":[{"text":"Direction, lanes, turns, speed, parking.","fact_ids":["sec04-F04"]},{"text":"Red circle and slash: banned.","fact_ids":["sec04-F04"]},{"text":"White rectangles flag special rules.","fact_ids":["sec04-F04"]}],"narration":{"text":"Other regulation signs rule direction, lane use, turns, speed, parking and special cases. A red circle with a slash across it bans the pictured action or vehicle, such as a turn or a type of vehicle. And rectangular white signs flag special rules that apply on that stretch of road. So when you see a red circle and slash, read it as no: whatever is pictured inside is not allowed. When you see a white rectangle, read it as a rule you must follow. Together with stop and yield, these are the signs that state the law, as opposed to the signs that warn or guide.","fact_ids":["sec04-F04"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec04-u01-s7","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Check the yield sign","fact_ids":["sec04-F03","sec04-R01"]},"lines":[{"text":"A yield sign, traffic approaching.","fact_ids":["sec04-F03","sec04-R01"]},{"text":"What must you do?","fact_ids":["sec04-F03","sec04-R01"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: you reach a yield sign and cross traffic is approaching close by. What must you do? Work it out before reading on. The answer is to slow down, check traffic, be ready to stop, and stop fully because conditions require it, yielding the right-of-way. If the way had been clear, you could have continued after slowing and checking. If you answered that a yield sign never requires a stop, that is the common mistake. The yield sign halts you only when traffic demands, while a stop sign halts you every single time, whatever the traffic.","fact_ids":["sec04-F03","sec04-R01"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec04-u01-s8","kind":"close","title":{"text":"Signs that state rules","fact_ids":["sec04-F01","sec04-F02","sec04-F03","sec04-F04"]},"lines":[{"text":"White, yellow, green, blue.","fact_ids":["sec04-F01","sec04-F02","sec04-F03","sec04-F04"]},{"text":"Stop always; yield when needed.","fact_ids":["sec04-F01","sec04-F02","sec04-F03","sec04-F04"]},{"text":"Circle and slash means no.","fact_ids":["sec04-F01","sec04-F02","sec04-F03","sec04-F04"]}],"narration":{"text":"To close, regulation signs are normally white rectangles with black or red markings, warnings are yellow diamonds with black, destinations are green with white, and services are blue with white. The stop sign demands a full stop with right-of-way yielded, before the stop line, else the crosswalk, else the nearest point with a clear view. The yield sign demands slowing, traffic checks, readiness to stop and a full stop when conditions require. Other regulation signs rule direction, lanes, turns, speed and parking, and a red circle and slash bans the pictured action. Next come warning, work, guide and service signs.","fact_ids":["sec04-F01","sec04-F02","sec04-F03","sec04-F04"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"}]},{"unit_id":"sec04-u02","module_id":"sec04-m02","objective_ids":["sec04-u02"],"title":{"text":"Warning, work and guide signs","fact_ids":["sec04-F05","sec04-R02","sec04-F06"]},"why_how":[{"text":"Yellow warnings advise, while orange work signs order.","fact_ids":["sec04-F05","sec04-F06","sec04-R02"]},{"text":"Green and blue signs guide you to places and services.","fact_ids":["sec04-F07","sec04-F08"]}],"worked_example":{"scenario":{"text":"Sam drives into a work zone where no speed limit is posted and a flagger holds up a signal.","fact_ids":["sec04-F06"]},"reasoning":{"text":"Drivers slow through every work zone and obey every flag signal with or without a posted limit.","fact_ids":["sec04-F06"]},"result":{"text":"Sam slows down and follows the flagger's signal.","fact_ids":["sec04-F06"]}},"misconception":{"claim":{"text":"Common mistake: thinking a work zone without a posted limit means you may keep your normal speed.","fact_ids":["sec04-F06"]},"correction":{"text":"Drivers slow through every work zone and obey every flag signal, with or without a posted limit.","fact_ids":["sec04-F06"]}},"memory_support":{"text":"Yellow advises, orange orders, green guides, blue serves.","fact_ids":["sec04-R02","sec04-F07","sec04-F08"]},"self_check":{"prompt":{"text":"You enter a work zone with no posted limit. What must you do?","fact_ids":["sec04-F06"]},"answer":{"text":"Slow down and obey every flag signal.","fact_ids":["sec04-F06"]},"rationale":{"text":"Orange work signs command slowdowns, unlike yellow warnings, which only advise.","fact_ids":["sec04-R02","sec04-F06"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec04-u02-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"Signs that warn and guide","fact_ids":["sec04-F05","sec04-F06","sec04-F07","sec04-F08"]},"lines":[{"text":"Yellow warnings, orange work signs.","fact_ids":["sec04-F05","sec04-F06","sec04-F07","sec04-F08"]},{"text":"Green destinations, blue services.","fact_ids":["sec04-F05","sec04-F06","sec04-F07","sec04-F08"]}],"narration":{"text":"This lesson covers the signs that warn you and the signs that guide you. Yellow-and-black warning signs point out hazards and special rules, sometimes with an advisory speed. Orange-and-black signs mark work zones, and the manual treats them more firmly. Green-and-white signs give direction and distance, and route markers name the kind of road by their shape. Blue-and-white signs point to services. The key contrast is between yellow and orange: one gives advice and the other gives orders. We will go through each family, then line up that contrast, then check your understanding with a work-zone question.","fact_ids":["sec04-F05","sec04-F06","sec04-F07","sec04-F08"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec04-u02-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Yellow warnings","fact_ids":["sec04-F05"]},"lines":[{"text":"Yellow-and-black mark hazards.","fact_ids":["sec04-F05"]},{"text":"Also special rules ahead.","fact_ids":["sec04-F05"]},{"text":"Advisory speed urges slower travel.","fact_ids":["sec04-F05"]}],"narration":{"text":"Yellow-and-black warning signs mark hazards and special rules on the road ahead. Sometimes a warning sign is paired with a yellow-and-black advisory speed, which urges you to travel more slowly. The word the manual uses for that speed is advisory, and the sign urges slower travel rather than setting a hard limit. So when you see a yellow warning, slow down and pay attention to whatever hazard or special rule it marks, and if an advisory speed is shown, take it as the slower pace recommended for that stretch. Keep in mind that the orange signs on the next slide work differently.","fact_ids":["sec04-F05"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":41,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec04-u02-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Orange work signs","fact_ids":["sec04-F06"]},"lines":[{"text":"Orange-and-black mark active work.","fact_ids":["sec04-F06"]},{"text":"Possible flag control; limits as low as twenty-five.","fact_ids":["sec04-F06"]},{"text":"Slow down; obey every flag signal.","fact_ids":["sec04-F06"]}],"narration":{"text":"Orange-and-black signs mark active work on or near the road. There may be flag control, and work zones can have speed limits as low as twenty-five. Drivers slow down through every work zone and obey every flag signal, whether or not a speed limit is posted. So the absence of a posted limit is not permission to keep your normal speed. If a flagger signals you to stop or slow, you do it. Orange tells you that people are working and that the rules there are orders you must follow, which is the main difference from the yellow warnings you just saw.","fact_ids":["sec04-F06"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":41,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec04-u02-s4","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Advice versus orders","fact_ids":["sec04-R02","sec04-F05","sec04-F06"]},"lines":[{"text":"Yellow: advisory speeds, caution.","fact_ids":["sec04-R02","sec04-F05","sec04-F06"]},{"text":"Orange: enforceable limits, flaggers.","fact_ids":["sec04-R02","sec04-F05","sec04-F06"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is the trap. Yellow and orange signs look similar, both with black markings, so people treat them the same way. The manual sets them apart. Yellow warnings advise caution with advisory speeds. Orange work signs command slowdowns with enforceable limits and flag obedience. It is advice versus orders. So a yellow advisory speed urges slower travel, while an orange work zone requires you to slow down and to obey any flagger, posted limit or not. If a question asks which sign carries enforceable limits and flaggers, the answer is the orange work sign, not the yellow warning.","fact_ids":["sec04-R02","sec04-F05","sec04-F06"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec04-u02-s5","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Green destinations and routes","fact_ids":["sec04-F07"]},"lines":[{"text":"Green-and-white: direction and distance.","fact_ids":["sec04-F07"]},{"text":"Route markers name road types by shape.","fact_ids":["sec04-F07"]},{"text":"Plan with a map; track en route.","fact_ids":["sec04-F07"]}],"narration":{"text":"Green-and-white destination signs give direction and distance to places. Route markers come in varied shapes, and the shape names the kind of road: interstate, United States, state or county. The manual's sample shows them in the order state, United States, interstate. These markers help with map planning before a trip and with keeping track of your route while you drive. So green signs and route markers are your navigation tools: green for where and how far, and the marker shape for what kind of road you are on. Use them together with your map to stay on course.","fact_ids":["sec04-F07"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec04-u02-s6","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Blue service signs","fact_ids":["sec04-F08","sec04-F01"]},"lines":[{"text":"Blue-and-white point to services.","fact_ids":["sec04-F08","sec04-F01"]},{"text":"Rest areas and fuel.","fact_ids":["sec04-F08","sec04-F01"]},{"text":"Camping and medical help.","fact_ids":["sec04-F08","sec04-F01"]}],"narration":{"text":"Blue-and-white service signs point to services along the road. The manual lists rest areas, fuel, camping and medical help. So when you need a break, gas, a place to camp, or medical care, look for blue. Together with the other families, you now have the whole color code: white regulation signs state rules, yellow warnings mark hazards, orange work signs order slowdowns, green destination signs give direction and distance, and blue service signs point to help and services. Knowing the color lets you sort a sign at a distance, long before you are close enough to read every word on it.","fact_ids":["sec04-F08","sec04-F01"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec04-u02-s7","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Check the work zone","fact_ids":["sec04-F06","sec04-R02"]},"lines":[{"text":"Work zone, no posted limit.","fact_ids":["sec04-F06","sec04-R02"]},{"text":"What must you do?","fact_ids":["sec04-F06","sec04-R02"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: you drive into a work zone where no speed limit is posted, and a flagger is directing traffic ahead. What must you do? Work it out before reading on. The answer is to slow down and obey every flag signal. The manual says drivers slow through every work zone and obey every flag signal with or without a posted limit. If you answered that you may keep your normal speed because no limit is posted, that is the common mistake. Orange work signs command slowdowns and flag obedience, while yellow warnings only advise caution.","fact_ids":["sec04-F06","sec04-R02"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec04-u02-s8","kind":"close","title":{"text":"Warn, order, guide, serve","fact_ids":["sec04-F05","sec04-F06","sec04-F07","sec04-F08","sec04-R02"]},"lines":[{"text":"Yellow advises; orange orders.","fact_ids":["sec04-F05","sec04-F06","sec04-F07","sec04-F08","sec04-R02"]},{"text":"Green guides; blue serves.","fact_ids":["sec04-F05","sec04-F06","sec04-F07","sec04-F08","sec04-R02"]}],"narration":{"text":"To wrap up, yellow-and-black warnings mark hazards and special rules, sometimes with a yellow-and-black advisory speed urging slower travel. Orange-and-black work signs mark active work with possible flag control and limits as low as twenty-five, and drivers slow through every work zone and obey every flag signal with or without a posted limit. Green-and-white destination signs give direction and distance, and route markers name interstate, United States, state or county roads by shape. Blue-and-white service signs point to rest areas, fuel, camping and medical help. Next we move from signs to traffic signals.","fact_ids":["sec04-F05","sec04-F06","sec04-F07","sec04-F08","sec04-R02"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":37,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"}]},{"unit_id":"sec04-u03","module_id":"sec04-m03","objective_ids":["sec04-u03"],"title":{"text":"Traffic signals and lane lights","fact_ids":["sec04-F09","sec04-F10","sec04-F11"]},"why_how":[{"text":"Each light, steady or flashing, round or arrow, has its own meaning.","fact_ids":["sec04-F09","sec04-F10","sec04-F11","sec04-F12","sec04-F13"]},{"text":"Turning on red depends on which red you face and where you are.","fact_ids":["sec04-F10","sec04-R03"]}],"worked_example":{"scenario":{"text":"Ivy stops at a steady red light outside the city and wants to turn right; no sign forbids it.","fact_ids":["sec04-F10"]},"reasoning":{"text":"Right on red is allowed after a full stop with yielding, except where signs, signals or markings forbid it.","fact_ids":["sec04-F10"]},"result":{"text":"Ivy stops fully, yields to traffic and pedestrians, then turns right.","fact_ids":["sec04-F10"]}},"misconception":{"claim":{"text":"Common mistake: thinking a red arrow allows a right turn after stopping, like a steady red.","fact_ids":["sec04-F11","sec04-R03"]},"correction":{"text":"A red arrow bans all movement its way until it clears, including any turn on red.","fact_ids":["sec04-F11","sec04-R03"]}},"memory_support":{"text":"Steady red, stop then maybe turn; red arrow, nothing; flashing red, stop sign.","fact_ids":["sec04-R03","sec04-F11"]},"self_check":{"prompt":{"text":"A traffic signal is flashing red. What does it mean for you?","fact_ids":["sec04-F11"]},"answer":{"text":"Treat it as a stop sign: stop, yield, then go when safe.","fact_ids":["sec04-F11"]},"rationale":{"text":"Flashing red copies the stop sign while flashing yellow only urges caution.","fact_ids":["sec04-R04","sec04-F11"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec04-u03-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"Lights that control traffic","fact_ids":["sec04-F09","sec04-F10","sec04-F11","sec04-F12","sec04-F13","sec04-F14"]},"lines":[{"text":"Steady, flashing, round and arrow.","fact_ids":["sec04-F09","sec04-F10","sec04-F11","sec04-F12","sec04-F13","sec04-F14"]},{"text":"Turns on red; overhead lane lights.","fact_ids":["sec04-F09","sec04-F10","sec04-F11","sec04-F12","sec04-F13","sec04-F14"]}],"narration":{"text":"This lesson covers traffic signals. The manual explains how signal lights are arranged, what to do when a signal is dark, and what each light means: steady red, flashing red, red arrows, steady and flashing yellow, yellow arrows, steady green and green arrows. It also covers turning on red, which depends on the kind of red and on where you are. Finally, there are overhead lane lights that open or close individual lanes. There is a lot here, so we will go light by light, then compare the look-alikes, and finish with a quick check on flashing signals.","fact_ids":["sec04-F09","sec04-F10","sec04-F11","sec04-F12","sec04-F13","sec04-F14"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec04-u03-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Steady red and turns on red","fact_ids":["sec04-F10"]},"lines":[{"text":"Stop until green, or a green arrow.","fact_ids":["sec04-F10"]},{"text":"Right on red after a full stop.","fact_ids":["sec04-F10"]},{"text":"Not where forbidden or unposted in the city.","fact_ids":["sec04-F10"]}],"narration":{"text":"A steady red light means stop and wait until it turns green, or move only in the direction of a green arrow when the way is clear. You may turn right on red, and turn left on red from a one-way street onto another one-way street, after a full stop and yielding. Those turns are not allowed where signs, signals or markings forbid them, anywhere in the city unless a sign permits it, and never for a school bus carrying students. So right on red is a permission with conditions: full stop first, yield, and no rule against it where you are.","fact_ids":["sec04-F10"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":41,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec04-u03-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Flashing red and red arrows","fact_ids":["sec04-F11"]},"lines":[{"text":"Flashing red equals a stop sign.","fact_ids":["sec04-F11"]},{"text":"Stop, yield, go when safe.","fact_ids":["sec04-F11"]},{"text":"Red arrow: no movement its way.","fact_ids":["sec04-F11"]}],"narration":{"text":"A flashing red light equals a stop sign. You stop, you yield, and you go when it is safe. A red arrow is stricter. It bans all movement in the direction it points until it clears, and that includes any turn on red. So if the right-turn arrow is red, you may not turn right even after a full stop, even though a steady round red would let you. The difference between a red arrow and a round red is the key point of this slide. A round steady red still allows certain turns after stopping, while a red arrow allows nothing its way.","fact_ids":["sec04-F11"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec04-u03-s4","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Three reds, three answers","fact_ids":["sec04-R03","sec04-F10","sec04-F11"]},"lines":[{"text":"Steady red: turns allowed after stopping.","fact_ids":["sec04-R03","sec04-F10","sec04-F11"]},{"text":"Red arrow: nothing its way.","fact_ids":["sec04-R03","sec04-F10","sec04-F11"]},{"text":"City red: nothing unless posted.","fact_ids":["sec04-R03","sec04-F10","sec04-F11"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is the trap. Every red looks like stop, so people assume they all work the same for turns. The manual gives three reds with three answers. A steady red allows right turns, and lefts from one-way to one-way, after stopping. A red arrow allows nothing its way. And in the city, a red allows nothing unless a sign permits the turn. So before you turn on red, ask which red you face and where you are. Round red outside the city, after a full stop, usually yes. Red arrow, no. City red without a sign allowing it, no. Three questions, three different answers.","fact_ids":["sec04-R03","sec04-F10","sec04-F11"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec04-u03-s5","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Yellows and greens","fact_ids":["sec04-F12","sec04-F13","sec04-R04"]},"lines":[{"text":"Steady yellow: red is coming.","fact_ids":["sec04-F12","sec04-F13","sec04-R04"]},{"text":"Flashing yellow: caution.","fact_ids":["sec04-F12","sec04-F13","sec04-R04"]},{"text":"Yellow arrow ends protection; green, yield.","fact_ids":["sec04-F12","sec04-F13","sec04-R04"]}],"narration":{"text":"A steady yellow light warns that red is about to appear, so prepare to stop. A flashing yellow light orders caution. A yellow arrow means the protection of a green arrow is ending, so drivers intending to turn should prepare to stop.
